c.tagline: Cradle of the Revolution — son and trova, Caribbean heat, and Sierra Maestra views.

taxi.fareNote: There is no Uber or ride-hailing in Cuba. Get around by state Cubataxi, shared fixed-route almendrones (classic American cars) and colectivos, or private taxis, always agreeing the fare before you set off. Fares for visitors are often quoted in USD cash; the informal dollar rate far exceeds the official peg, so carry small bills.

emergency.note: 106 reaches the police and 104 the ambulance service; response can be slow, and most casas and hotels will help arrange private medical care for visitors.

hood_landmark.Ferreiro: Plaza de Ferreiro, Santiago de Cuba
hood_landmark.Tivoli: Padre Pico staircase, Santiago de Cuba

avoid.reason: Persistent jinetero hustlers, bag-snatching and overcharging around Parque Céspedes and on dark streets at night.

hood_desc: The colonial core around Parque Cespedes, with the cathedral, Casa de Diego Velazquez and Hotel Casa Granda; the most walkable base for sights, live music and street life.
Santiago's oldest quarter, climbing the hills above the bay via the Padre Pico staircase, with French-Haitian heritage and a claim as the birthplace of trova and son; atmospheric and bohemian.
A leafy district of 1920s neoclassical mansions southeast of the centre, home to embassies, museums and the Melia Santiago; quieter and more upscale.
A calm residential area near the Moncada Barracks and the Plaza de la Revolucion, with a local feel and budget casas particulares.
A busy modern junction south of the centre around the Plaza de Ferreiro, with shops, transport links and hotels along Avenida de las Americas.

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled/filtered water; supply and quality are unreliable.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5:00-22:00 with a sharp evening drop-off; after dark, private taxis and classic cars are the main option.
transit.note: There is no metro, tram or urban rail; Santiago's hilly historic core is best explored on foot, with taxis for longer hops out to Vista Alegre or the Castillo del Morro.
transit.pay: City buses (guaguas) take a few pesos CUP in cash on board, but they are crowded and unreliable because of fuel shortages; most visitors use shared almendrones on fixed routes, private taxis or bicitaxis, agreeing the fare in cash beforehand.

ferry: Harbour launch (lancha) to Cayo Granma island
train: Ferrocarriles de Cuba services from Santiago station (long, slow trains to Havana and other provinces)

transit.m: State taxi to city centre (~15-20 min, agree fare first)
Shared taxi / almendron toward the centre (infrequent)

tip.r: Not expected, but rounding up or leaving about 10% (ideally in cash/USD) for good service is appreciated, and tipping musicians and guides is customary.
